newsitem.title: UK: Bigger G7 role for Russia may be part of NATO deal.
newsitem.headline: Bigger G7 role for Russia may be part of NATO deal.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
Russia may win a bigger role in the key forum grouping the world's rich nations to help it accept NATO enlargement, but diplomats say full membership for Moscow is out of the question for now.

Russia has pressed hard to join the Group of Seven (G7), an exclusive club which brings together the United States, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Italy and Britain. So far, Moscow has been admitted to political discussions only.

President Boris Yeltsin, who meets U.S. President Bill Clinton for a summit in Helsinki next week, raised the issue again recently with Germany -- Moscow's closest European ally -- as part of the negotiations on NATO enlargement.

Russia bitterly opposes the alliance's plans to take in new members from Central and Eastern Europe, seeing it as a direct threat to its own security. It is the main issue for next week's Helsinki summit.
Diplomats said most G7 countries were still reluctant to admit Russia as a full member of the rich nations' club, given its economic and political problems.

Nevertheless, they said it was likely Russia could be given a bigger role by formally including it not only in the political discussions at G7 summits but also in consultations on "global issues" such as crime, the environment and terrorism.
"Extending Russian participation is the key...but full membership is not on for now," said one Western diplomat.
In Helsinki, Clinton could announce broader Russian involvement at the next G7 summit along these lines as part of his initiative to woo Moscow over NATO enlargement.

The United States is hosting the next group summit, which will be held in the city of Denver on June 20-22 -- just over two weeks before a NATO summit in Madrid which will issue invitations to potential new members.
Russia has already taken part in discussions on nuclear safety, hosting a meeting in Moscow a year ago, and it has also been involved in talks on how to combat terrorism.

"The aim would be to formalise Russian participation in all of this, since they have much to contribute," said a Western diplomat, who asked not to be identified. "Pretty much everyone can accept that."

Another diplomat said: "The Russian mafia is the subject of increasing concern around the world. Why not have the Russians participate fully in discussions on issues like transnational crime and the environment?"

The West is already looking at a package of measures to sweeten the pill on NATO enlargement, with the aim of winning Russian acceptance -- however grudging -- before the alliance's Madrid summit in July.

The package includes a NATO-Russia agreement on security consultations, on which progress has been made, further cuts in arms levels and possibly more Western financial aid to show support for continued reforms.
Whether this, coupled with an expanded Russian role in the G7, will be enough remains to be seen.
Kremlin leaders have attended the group's summit meetings since 1991, taking part in a gradually growing proportion of the political section of the talks.
Yeltsin was fighting for a second term in elections at the time of last year's summit in Lyon, France, so he sent Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in his place.

Germany has gone further than its partners in arguing that the G7 should expand to include Russia and become the G8. This, Bonn argues, would be a small price to pay for making Moscow feel more secure about NATO enlargement.
But others are more wary and Japan is deeply suspicious of any deal linked to NATO, since -- unlike other G7 members -- it has nothing to do with the alliance, diplomats say.

In addition, Japan and Russia remain locked in a territorial dispute over the Kuriles, a string of small islands between northern Japan and Russia, since Soviet troops seized them in the closing days of World War Two.
Without the formal agreement of all G7 members, there is no prospect of Russia or any other country joining the club.
